Human in the Loop

Putting a human decision inside an automated claims flow.

AI workflowsHITLB2B SaaSInsurance
Surface
Web-based tool
Role
Solo product designer, end to end
Team
Solo product designer (me), product manager, engineering and ML partners
Scope
UX · Interaction design · Human-in-the-loop systems
Timeline
6 weeks

Problem

The verification bottleneck

Whenever a claim triggered a low-confidence AI decision, handlers had to manually re-verify it, jumping between the CRM, email, and PDF viewers, and scanning full documents to find a single data point. It took 40 to 50 minutes per claim.

Solution

A review step builders place on the canvas

Builders add a HITL block on the canvas that pauses a claim and routes it on the reviewer's decision. Reviewers work in a Human Review tab in Flow Details, next to Connected apps and Logs. There they see the email, every attached document and all the AI's predictions with confidence scores, ready to edit on one page. They can check and correct values without jumping between email and PDF viewers.

Result

Review time down 94%

Claim reviews dropped from 40 to 50 minutes to under 3. Within three months, 90% fewer claims needed a human at all.

Measured with an insurance client over the first three months after launch, using the time between Received On and Reviewed On for each case. Data shared by the Simplifai solutions team.

About

Where HITL fits

Simplifai's Flow Builder lets claims teams chain AI skills into automated intake workflows. But automation is only as trustworthy as the moments where it hands control back to a person.

This case study is about that handoff: the Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) system I designed as the review layer sitting behind every flow. It covers how builders add and configure the block, how runs pause, and how reviewers work through the queue.

Problem

Every unsure AI decision cost a handler 40 to 50 minutes

When the AI made a low-confidence decision on a claim, a handler had to check it by hand. They jumped between the CRM, the email and PDF viewers, and scanned whole documents to find a single data point.

The tooling made it worse. Review sat outside Flow Builder as a separate post-processing step, so builders could not choose where a person steps in. Reviewers could only approve or reject. No screen showed the email, its attachments and the AI's output together.

That limited trust in AI decisions, and it limited how much teams were willing to automate.

Why solve it now

  • Cost and compliance. Rising pressure across the industry to cut claims-handling cost while improving compliance and audit readiness.
  • Trust. Teams need a structured, confidence-aware way for people to control AI decisions before automating more.
  • One system. Configuration, execution, human review and routing lived in separate places. HITL connects them.

Objective

Design the mandatory Human-in-the-Loop system so it functions as a trust layer, not a compliance checkbox, turning a legal requirement into a feature that accelerates enterprise adoption.

Sarah, Claims Handler, 31, Oslo

"I spend more time copying and pasting than I do talking to customers or making decisions."

Flow builders

HITL user stories
Claims handlerFlow builder (solutions team)Business
  • As a claims handler, I want low-confidence AI decisions to pause for my review, so that I can correct them before the claim moves on.
  • As a claims handler, I want to see the email, every attachment and the AI’s predictions on one page, so that I don’t jump between apps to verify a claim.
  • As a claims handler, I want to see how confident the AI is in each value, so that I can focus on the fields most likely to be wrong.
  • As a claims handler, I want to edit, replace or clear a predicted value, so that the correct data is passed on to the next step.
  • As a claims handler, I want a queue of pending and reviewed cases, so that I can track and prioritise my work.
  • As a claims handler, I want to choose from actions that match our process, so that each claim takes the right next step.
  • As a flow builder, I want each reviewer action to become its own branch, so that the flow continues based on the decision.
  • As a flow builder, I want logs to show when a run is awaiting review, so that I know where and why a flow paused.
  • As a claims operations lead, I want to cut handling time per claim, so that my team can process more claims without adding staff.
  • As a company, I want every uncertain AI decision to have a clear human checkpoint, so that we stay compliant and audit-ready.

HITL user flowScroll sideways on small screens

Sketching the review page before Figma

I started on whiteboards. The first question was what a reviewer needs at first glance: the case ID, its status, the category the AI predicted with its confidence, the extracted fields, and the source document right beside them.

What carried into the final design

  • Tabs for the email and each attachment became the file chip strip.
  • Category and extracted fields next to the viewer became File Insights and Global Extract.
  • Predicted values with a confidence score became the confidence badges.
  • Highlighting what the AI predicted became the multiple values and human-edited markers.

What changed

  • A single Approve button became 1 to 5 reviewer actions that the builder defines.
  • Bulk approval stayed out of the MVP, so every case gets its own decision.
Core idea

A human decision as a block in the flow

Instead of a review layer on the side, HITL is a block that builders place, configure and connect like any other. When a run reaches it, the flow pauses and a review record is created. When the reviewer acts, the flow resumes on the branch for that action.

Flow runsClassify and extract
→
HITL pausesLog shows Awaiting Review
→
Reviewer actsChecks, corrects, picks an action
→
Flow resumesOn the chosen branch

Actions become branches

Builders name 1 to 5 reviewer actions, such as "Submit claim" or "Send to specialist". On Save, each name becomes a labelled branch. The same names appear in the reviewer's Take Action menu and as queue filters, so the builder's intent and the reviewer's choice stay in sync.

The block exists the moment you drop it

Picking HITL from the Logic tab places the block with default settings and opens the configuration modal. Save updates the block. Cancel changes nothing. That one rule removed a whole class of edge cases.

Protecting the builder's work

Deleting an action can destroy every step under its branch. My first version asked for an explicit confirmation. In review, the tech lead pointed out that a double confirmation leaves people unsure when the delete happens. I changed it to delete with an undo: the row is greyed out, a warning appears with Restore all, and nothing is final until Save.

Inserting HITL mid-flow or deleting a HITL block can also break an existing flow. A modal only appears when there is a real choice to make:

Deleting a HITL block withWhat happens
2+ actions, a branch has stepsModal Builder picks which branch to keep
2+ actions, no stepsInstant Block removed
1 action with stepsInstant Steps move up to the previous node
1 action, no stepsInstant Block removed
The review page

Context, confidence and control in one place

One claim can arrive as an email plus several attachments. A chip strip lists each file. Switching chips updates the viewer and the File Insights, which hold classifications per document. Global Extract on the right holds case-level fields and stays put when you switch files. The layout matches how the data works: document type belongs to a file, policy number belongs to the claim.

Each field state tells the reviewer where to look and what they can do:

Field stateWhat the reviewer seesWhat they can do
PredictedValue with a confidence badgeKeep it, or open other predictions with their scores
Multiple candidatesMultiple values icon with tooltipCompare candidates and pick one
No matchEmpty classification, all options at 0 confidencePick a defined value or None
Human editedHuman badge on the fieldType a new value, or switch back to a prediction
ClearedEmpty field with human badge, no errorProceed with no value, or restore a prediction
After actionRead-only fields, icons hiddenBrowse files, zoom and download only

Every change saves automatically. Marking human edits keeps a visible line between what the model said and what a person decided.

Decisions are deliberate and final

Take Action lists the builder's action names. Choosing one opens a short confirmation. On confirm, the flow resumes, the log updates, and the page locks into view mode. Undo was out of scope for the MVP, so the confirmation step matters.

I later refined the queue for teams. An "In review" column shows who has a case open. The page says "You are reviewing this case since…", and a Hand back button releases it. That prevents two people working on the same claim.

Learnings

Writing the spec was design work too

Describe behaviour, not implementation

My first stories said a unique block ID was "generated on Save". Engineering pointed out that this is a technical detail, and it was also wrong. I now write what the user sees and leave the how to engineering.

One rule beats many exceptions

"Nothing is saved on Cancel" removed a whole set of edge cases. A clear model is easier to design, build and test.

Don't remove what the user just created

An early idea removed empty action fields when they lost focus. We kept them and showed an inline error instead. Surprising people costs more than an extra error state.

Left out of the MVP on purpose: undo, SLA-based auto decisions, role-based access per action, edit audit logs, and reordering actions.
